newsitem.title: perU: Fresh Peru hostage talks as rebels defiant.
newsitem.headline: Fresh Peru hostage talks as rebels defiant.

text.p: Peru's government and Marxist rebels began fresh negotiations over the fate of 72 hostages on Wednesday after the guerrillas warned in advance they would resist the bait of asylum in Cuba to lure them out.

As the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) representative was driven in a Red Cross car to a safe house for the talks, guerrilla comrades defiantly sang "The Mills," a song about a bloody battle with security forces.

The ninth round of talks could mark the beginning of real bargaining in the 78-day siege, after President Alberto Fujimori said on Tuesday that the government planned to present an "all-inclusive proposal" to the Tupac Amaru.

But before Fujimori spoke, rebel chief Nestor Cerpa served notice the guerrillas were holding firm to their chief demand -- the release of 400 jailed comrades -- and would not simply accept the government's offers of safe passage to Cuba.

Cerpa said the first eight rounds of talks had led only to both sides repeating their positions and that the lack of progress toward a deal had led him not to attend the most recent session on Monday, sending his second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, instead.

"We believe this (the talks) cannot continue indefinitely in the sense that they can get worn down and lose a certain level of legitimacy," Cerpa warned, speaking by walkie-talkie from within the captured Japanese ambassador's residence.

In another show of combative rebel spirits as the unidentified MRTA negotiator was driven to the talks, two of the 20-odd guerrillas clambered on to the mansion's roof to rearrange anti-government banners and the Tupac Amaru flag.
"On the 78th day of the capture of the Japanese ambassador's residence, nobody is surrendering here, damn it!" the guerrillas yelled.
Opposition daily La Republica cited official sources saying the government's "all-inclusive proposal" includes guarantees it will not seek to extradite the rebels if they fly to asylum.

Although the government will stand by its refusal to free any prisoners, the proposal does not rule out the possibility that Fujimori might eventually grant amnesties to MRTA members, La Republica reported.
Fujimori has hinted at other concessions, possibly including a softening of harsh conditions for MRTA prisoners and reform of trial processes.

Key to government strategy for finding a bloodless way out to Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis is the prospect of asylum in Cuba or the Dominican Republic for the rebels holed up in the mansion.
Fujimori took a planeload of journalists with him on a surprise trip to the Caribbean on Sunday and Monday, and secured an offer by Cuban leader Fidel Castro to accept the rebels if all sides agree.
But, in a statement sent to Reuters via electronic-mail early on Wednesday, the MRTA repeated its demands, and slammed Fujimori's "dictatorship" for "atrocious" jail conditions.

The statement from the MRTA's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco criticised "the toughening of jail conditions, the suspension of the 30-minute visits once a month, the lack of medical attention, the denial of entry for the Red Cross, the physical and psychological tortures."

The MRTA said it sought a "political and peaceful solution" to the crisis, but talks were dragging on because the government was distracted by attempts to "justify itself and look for those responsible for negligence" in the seizure of the residence.

The rebels initially grabbed more than 500 captives at a cocktail party to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday on Dec. 17. The remaining hostages include Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two government ministers, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
